```{r, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(readr)
library(rworldmap)
library(plotly)
library(GGally)
```

# Data

Data Load the data set you exported in the final Task of Case Study 2.
Eliminate all observations with missing values in the income status
variable. As a reminder, the data set contains information on

-   median age
-   youth unemployment rate
-   net migration rate (difference between the number of persons
    entering and leaving a country during the year per 1,000 persons -
    based on midyear population)

for most world entities. The data was downloaded from
<https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/about/archives/>. Additional
information on continent, subcontinent and income status was appended to
the dataset in Case Study 2.

# Tasks

<!-- Block 1 -->

#### Data loading
```{r, message=FALSE}
file_path <- "../data/final_dataset.csv"

# Load the CSV file into a data frame
df <- read.csv(file_path, sep = ";", na.strings = ".", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Eliminate all observations with missing values in the income_status variable
df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(income_status))

# Transform income_status variable to factor
df <- df %>%
  mutate(income_status = factor(income_status, levels = c("H", "UM", "LM", "L")))
```


## a) Median age in different income levels

```{=html}
<!-- Using ggplot2, create a density plot of the median age grouped by income status groups. The densities for the different groups are superimposed in the same plot rather than in different plots. Ensure that you order the levels of the income status such that in the plots the legend is ordered from High (H) to Low (L).

- The color of the density lines is black.
- The area under the density curve should be colored differently among the income status levels.
- For the colors, choose a transparency level of 0.5 for better visibility.
- Position the legend at the top center of the plot and give it no title (hint: use element_blank()).
- Rename the x axis as “Median age of population”

Comment briefly on the plot.-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(df, aes(x = median_age, fill = income_status, color = income_status)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = "black") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Median age of population") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = FALSE), color = guide_legend(reverse = FALSE))
```

In this plot, we observe a positive correlation between the median age of the population and the income status of the country. Specifically, low-income countries tend to have a lower median age, while high-income countries tend to have a higher median age. This trend is particularly evident in low-income countries, where the distribution is narrow (indicating low standard deviation) with a mean around 20 years old. In contrast, high-income countries have a peak around 43 years old.

## b) Income status in different continents
```{=html}
<!-- Investigate how the income status is distributed in the different continents.

- Using ggplot2, create a stacked barplot of absolute frequencies showing how the entities are split into continents and income status. Comment the plot.
-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
df_cleaned <- df %>% filter(!is.na(Continent))
# Create a stacked barplot of absolute frequencies
ggplot(df_cleaned, aes(x = Continent, fill = income_status)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Continent", y = "Count", fill = "Income Status") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Income Status Across Continents (Absolute Frequencies)")
```

In this plot, we can first observe the number of countries analyzed for each continent, as we are working with absolute frequencies. Africa has the most countries, while South America has the fewest. Additionally, we see the distribution of income status within each continent. Africa has a significant number of low-income and low-medium income countries, followed by Asia. In contrast, Europe has a majority of high-income countries, no low-income countries, and very few low-medium income countries.

```{=html}
<!-- 
- Create another stacked barplot of relative frequencies (height of the bars should be one). Comment the plot.
-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Create a data frame with relative frequencies
df_rel_freq <- df_cleaned %>%
  group_by(Continent, income_status) %>%
  summarise(count = n()) %>%
  mutate(rel_freq = count / sum(count))

# Create a stacked barplot of relative frequencies
ggplot(df_rel_freq, aes(x = Continent, y = rel_freq, fill = income_status)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Continent", y = "Relative Frequency", fill = "Income Status") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Income Status Across Continents (Relative Frequencies)")
```

In this plot, since we are working with relative frequencies, we don't have information about the number of countries in each continent.  However, it gives us a clearer picture of how income status is distributed within each continent. This makes it easier to compare income levels across continents. For instance, we can see that a higher percentage of South American countries fall under the high-medium income category compared to Europe, North America, or Oceania.

```{=html}
<!-- 
- Create a mosaic plot of continents and income status using base R functions.
-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Create a contingency table
contingency_table <- table(df$Continent, df$income_status)

# Create a mosaic plot
mosaicplot(contingency_table,
  main = "Mosaic Plot of Continents and Income Status",
  xlab = "Continent", ylab = "Income Status", col = rainbow(length(unique(df$income_status)))
)
```

```{=html}
<!-- 
- Briefly comment on the differences between the three plots generated to investigate the income distribution among the different continents.
-->
```

- The absolute frequency plot shows the actual number of entities in each income status category within each continent. It is useful for understanding the raw counts and identifying which continents have more entities in certain income status categories.

- The relative frequency plot normalizes the data within each continent, providing a proportional view. This helps in comparing the composition of income status categories across continents, irrespective of the total number of entities in each continent.

- The mosaic plot offers a different perspective by displaying the association between two categorical variables. It combines both the count and proportion information, making it easier to compare the distribution of income status within each continent and across different continents simultaneously.

## c) Income status in different subcontinents
```{=html}
<!-- For Asia, investigate further how the income status distribution is in the different subcontinents. Use one of
the plots in b. for this purpose. Comment on the results. -->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
asia_df <- df %>% filter(Continent == "Asia")

# Create a stacked barplot of absolute frequencies
ggplot(asia_df, aes(x = Region_1, fill = income_status)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Subregion", y = "Count", fill = "Income Status") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Income Status Across Subregions in Asia (Absolute Frequencies)")
```

From this plot, we can observe differences across various sub-regions in Asia. Western Asia has the most countries and is the wealthiest region, followed by Eastern Asia, where most countries have high or upper-middle income, although some low-income countries are still present. In contrast, Central Asia and, especially, Southern Asia are poorer regions, with most countries falling into the low or lower-middle income categories.

## d) Net migration in different continents
```{=html}
<!-- 
- Using ggplot2, create parallel boxplots showing the distribution of the net migration rate in the
different continents.
- Prettify the plot (change y-, x-axis labels, etc).
- Identify which country in Asia constitutes the largest negative outlier and which country in Asia
constitutes the largest positive outlier.
- Comment on the plot.
-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Create parallel boxplots
p <- ggplot(df_cleaned, aes(x = Continent, y = net_migration_rate)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Continent", y = "Net Migration Rate",
    title = "Distribution of Net Migration Rate by Continent"
  )


# Identify the largest negative outlier
negative_outlier <- asia_df %>%
  filter(net_migration_rate == min(net_migration_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

# Identify the largest positive outlier
positive_outlier <- asia_df %>%
  filter(net_migration_rate == max(net_migration_rate, na.rm = TRUE))


# Add the outlier points with labels
p <- p +
  geom_point(data = negative_outlier, aes(x = Continent, y = net_migration_rate), color = "blue", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = negative_outlier, aes(x = Continent, y = net_migration_rate, label = country_name), vjust = -1, color = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = positive_outlier, aes(x = Continent, y = net_migration_rate), color = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = positive_outlier, aes(x = Continent, y = net_migration_rate, label = country_name), vjust = 1.5, color = "red")

# Print the plot
print(p)

# Print the outliers
print(negative_outlier)
print(positive_outlier)
```

In this plot, we observe the distribution of net migration rates across different continents. Europe, being a high-income continent, generally exhibits a positive net migration rate, indicating that more people are entering than leaving. However, the overall plot reveals that each continent has both positive and negative outliers, providing a mixed view of migration patterns. Exceptions to this trend are Oceania and South America. Oceania demonstrates substantial emigration, with consistently low net migration rates, while South America exhibits minimal migration movement overall. Additionally, Asia has two very significant outliers (Syria and Lebanon), highlighting extreme migration patterns within the continent due to instability in that area.

## e) Net migration in different subcontinents
```{=html}
<!-- 
The graph in d. clearly does not convey the whole picture. It would be interesting also to look at the
subcontinents, as it is likely that a lot of migration flows happen within the continent.
- Investigate the net migration in different subcontinents using again parallel boxplots. Group the
boxplots by continent (hint: use facet_grid with scales = "free_x").
- Remember to prettify the plot (rotate axis labels if needed).
- Describe what you see.
-->
```
```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(df_cleaned, aes(x = Region_1, y = net_migration_rate)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Subcontinent", y = "Net Migration Rate",
    title = "Net Migration Rate by Subcontinent and Continent"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) +
  facet_grid(~Continent, scales = "free_x")
```

In this plot, we explore migration flows within each continent, highlighting regional differences. In Africa, the variation in net migration rates is less pronounced. However, in Europe, there is a clear pattern of emigration from Eastern Europe to Western Europe, with Northern and Southern Europe also showing positive but less significant net migration rates. In North America, Northern America has the highest net migration rate, while the Caribbean and Central America regions experience more emigration. The differences are particularly striking in Oceania, where Australia and New Zealand see high immigration rates, while Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia experience high emigration rates. Asia presents an interesting case in Western Asia, with Lebanon showing a very high emigration rate and Syria a very high immigration rate, suggesting a possible migration flow between these neighboring countries.

## f) Median net migration rate per subcontinent
<!-- The plot in task e. shows the distribution of the net migration rate for each subcontinent. Here you will work on visualizing only one summary statistic, namely the median.
For each subcontinent, calculate the median net migration rate. Then create a plot which contains the sub-regions on the y-axis and the median net migration rate on the x-axis.
- As geoms use points.
- Color the points by continent – use a colorblind friendly palette (see e.g. http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/Colors_(ggplot2)/).
- Rename the axes.
- Using fct_reorder from the forcats package, arrange the levels of subcontinent such that in the plot the lowest (bottom) subcontinent contains the lowest median net migration rate and the upper most region contains the highest median net migration rate.
- Comment on the plot. E.g., what are the regions with the most influx? What are the regions with the most outflux? -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
df_summary <- df_cleaned %>%
  group_by(Region_1, Continent) %>%
  summarise(median_migration = median(net_migration_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(df_summary, aes(x = fct_reorder(Region_1, median_migration), y = median_migration, color = Continent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    x = "Subcontinent", y = "Median Net Migration Rate",
    title = "Median Net Migration by Region",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_flip()
```

It is not difficult to recognise regions with high *influx* and *outflux* of migrants. Surprises Australia and New Zealand, which have the highest inwards value. On the other hand, and belonging to the same continent, Polynesia and Micronesia have the highest outflux median (possibly some of these migrants end up in Australia/New Zealand...). Other interesting aspects are: Europe is the only continent where all its subregions have a positive median net migration rate, and Africa is the only continent where all its subregions have a negative median net migration rate.

## g) Median youth unemployment rate per subcontinent
<!-- For each subcontinent, calculate the median youth unemployment rate. Then create a plot which contains the sub-regions on the y-axis and the median unemployment rate on the x-axis.
- Use a black and white theme (?theme_bw())
- As geoms use bars. (hint: pay attention to the statistical transformation taking place in geom_bar() – look into argument stat="identity")
- Color the bars by continent – use a colorblind friendly palette.
- Make the bars transparent (use alpha = 0.7).
- Rename the axes.
- Using fct_reorder from the forcats package, arrange the levels of subcontinent such that in the plot the lowest (bottom) subcontinent contains the lowest median youth unemployment rate and the upper most region contains the highest median youth unemployment rate.
- Comment on the plot. E.g., what are the regions with the highest vs lowest youth unemployment rate? -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
df_sum_empl <- df_cleaned %>%
  group_by(Region_1, Continent) %>%
  summarise(median_unemployment = median(youth_unempl_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(df_sum_empl, aes(x = fct_reorder(Region_1, median_unemployment), y = median_unemployment, fill = Continent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    x = "Subcontinent", y = "Median Youth Unemployment Rate",
    title = "Median Youth Unemployment Rate by Region",
    fill = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  coord_flip()
```

Regions with the highest median unemployment rate are Southern and Northern Africa, followed by Polynesia and (unsurprisingly) Southern Europe. Regions with the lowest median unemployment rate are Eastern, Central and South-eastern Asia, closely followed by Western Africa.


## h) Median youth unemployment rate per subcontinent – with error bars
<!-- The value displayed in the barplot in g. is the result of an aggregation, so it might be useful to also plot error bars, to have a general idea on how precise the median unemployment is. This can be achieved by plotting the error bars which reflect the standard deviation or the interquartile range of the variable in each of the subcontinents.
Repeat the plot in h. but include also error bars which reflect the 25% and 75% quantiles. You can use geom_errorbar in ggplot2. -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
df_sum_empl <- df_cleaned %>%
  group_by(Region_1, Continent) %>%
  summarise(
    median_unemployment = median(youth_unempl_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = quantile(youth_unempl_rate, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper = quantile(youth_unempl_rate, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(df_sum_empl, aes(x = fct_reorder(Region_1, median_unemployment), y = median_unemployment, fill = Continent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    x = "Subcontinent", y = "Median Youth Unemployment Rate",
    title = "Median Youth Unemployment Rate by Region",
    fill = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  coord_flip()
```

The added error bar only helps estimate the size of the subregion. Polynesia will have many countries, thus the high error bar, while Australia/New Zealand are only two, hence the almost non-existent error bar.


## i) Relationship between median age and net migration rate
<!-- Using ggplot2, create a plot showing the relationship between median age and net migration rate.
- Color the geoms based on the income status.
- Add a regression line for each development status (using geom_smooth()).
Comment on the plot. Do you see any relationship between the two variables? Do you see any difference among the income levels? -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
df_cleaned %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = net_migration_rate, y = median_age, color = income_status)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Net migration rate", y = "Median age", color = "Income Status") +
  theme_bw()


df_cleaned %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = net_migration_rate, y = median_age, color = income_status)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-20, 20)) +
  labs(x = "Net migration rate", y = "Median age", color = "Income Status") +
  theme_bw()
```

Looking at the first graph is not really helpful, so the same information is shown in the second, just with the x axis clipped to \(\pm 20\). It is difficult to say whether a relation exists between net migration rate and median age. Points are really scattered and the regression lines, although fitted, do not represent the data very well. The only clear information that can be extracted is the median age based on income level. Low income countries have low median age, while high income countries have higher median age. Upper-middle and low-middle income countries are in between, but the relation is not so clear.

## k) Merging population data
<!-- Go online and find a data set which contains the 2020 population for the countries of the world together with ISO codes.
- Download this data and merge it to the dataset you are working on in this case study using a left join. (A possible source: World Bank))
- Inspect the data and check whether the join worked well. -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load the population data
population_data <- read_csv("../data/total_population.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Select only the relevant columns: Country Code and 2020 [YR2020]
population_data <- population_data %>% select(`Country Code`, `2020 [YR2020]`)

# Rename columns for easier merging
population_data <- population_data %>%
  rename(GENC = `Country Code`, Population = `2020 [YR2020]`)

# Merge the population data with the existing dataset
merged_df <- df %>%
  left_join(population_data, by = "GENC")

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
  mutate(Population = as.numeric(Population))

# Inspect the dataset

# head(merged_df)

# summary(merged_df)
# str(merged_df)

# missing_population <- merged_df %>% filter(is.na(Population))
# print(missing_population)
```

## l) Scatterplot of median age and net migration rate in Europe
<!-- Make a scatterplot of median age and net migration rate for the countries of Europe. * Scale the size of the points according to each country’s population.
- For better visibility, use a transparency of alpha=0.7.
- Remove the legend.
- Comment on the plot. -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Filter the dataset to include only European countries
europe_data <- merged_df %>% filter(Continent == "Europe")

# Create the scatter plot
ggplot(europe_data, aes(x = net_migration_rate, y = median_age, size = Population)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "blue") +  
  labs(
    x = "Net Migration Rate",
    y = "Median Age",
    title = "Scatterplot of Median Age and Net Migration Rate in Europe"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +  
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",  
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),  
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),  
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray", size = 0.5),  
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()  
  )
```

Most countries cluster around a median age of 40 to 45 years and a net migration rate close to zero, indicating stable migration patterns. There are a few outliers with higher net migration rates and varying median ages, reflecting diverse migration trends across Europe. This plot effectively highlights the central tendencies and differences in demographics and migration within Europe.

## m) Interactive plot
<!-- On the merged data set from Task k., using function ggplotly from package plotly re-create the scatterplot in Task l., but this time for all countries. Color the points according to their continent.
When hovering over the points the name of the country, the values for median age, net migration rate, and population should be shown. (Hint: use the aesthetic text = Country. In ggplotly use the argument tooltip = c("text", "x", "y", "size")). -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Create the scatter plot using ggplot2
p <- ggplot(merged_df, aes(x = net_migration_rate, y = median_age, size = Population, color = Continent, text = country_name)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +  
  labs(
    x = "Net Migration Rate",
    y = "Median Age",
    title = "Scatterplot of Median Age and Net Migration Rate for All Countries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +  
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",  
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),  
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12)  
  )

# Convert the ggplot object to a plotly object for interactivity
interactive_plot <- ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("text", "x", "y", "size"))

interactive_plot
```

## n) Parallel coordinate plot
<!-- In parallel coordinate plots each observation or data point is depicted as a line traversing a series of parallel axes, corresponding to a specific variable or dimension. It is often used for identifying clusters in the data.
One can create such a plot using the GGally R package. You should create such a plot where you look at the three main variables in the data set: median age, youth unemployment rate and net migration rate. Color the lines based on the income status. Briefly comment. -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Filter the dataset to select the relevant columns
parallel_df <- merged_df %>%
  select(median_age, youth_unempl_rate, net_migration_rate, income_status)

# Create the parallel coordinate plot
p <- ggparcoord(
  data = parallel_df,
  columns = 1:3,  
  groupColumn = 4,  
  scale = "uniminmax",  
  alphaLines = 0.3  
) +
  labs(
    title = "Parallel Coordinate Plot of Median Age, Youth Unemployment Rate, and Net Migration Rate",
    x = "Variables",
    y = "Scaled Values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +  
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),  
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),  
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),  
    legend.position = "bottom"  
  )

print(p)
```

High-income countries generally have higher median ages and lower youth unemployment rates, while low-income countries have lower median ages and higher youth unemployment rates. The net migration rate varies widely within each income group, with high-income countries experiencing both higher and lower rates. Low-income countries tend to cluster around lower net migration rates.

The values 1.00, 0.75, 0.50, 0.25, and 0.00 on the y-axis, represent the scaled values of the variables (median_age, youth_unempl_rate, and net_migration_rate), these allow for a direct comparison between different units.

## o) World map visualisation
<!-- Using the package rworldmap, create a world map of the median age per country. Use the vignette https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rworldmap/vignettes/rworldmap.pdf to find how to do this in R. -->
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# install.packages("rworldmap")

# Prepare the data
merged_df2 <- merged_df %>%
  select(GENC, median_age) %>%
  rename(ISO3 = GENC)

# Join your data with the world map data
sPDF <- joinCountryData2Map(merged_df2, joinCode = "ISO3", nameJoinColumn = "ISO3")

# Define a more distinct color palette
colorPalette <- colorRampPalette(c("lightyellow", "yellow", "orange", "red3", "darkred"))

# Plot the world map
mapCountryData(sPDF, nameColumnToPlot = "median_age", 
               mapTitle = "World Map of Median Age per Country",
               colourPalette = colorPalette(20), 
               oceanCol = "lightblue", 
               missingCountryCol = "gray",
               borderCol = "gray", 
               addLegend = TRUE)

legend("bottomleft", legend = round(seq(min(sPDF$median_age, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                        max(sPDF$median_age, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                        length.out = 10), 1), 
       fill = colorPalette(10), 
       title = "Median Age",
       cex = 0.8, 
       bty = "n")
```
